Abstract:

In contemporary discourse, Kashmir is mapped either as a zone of protracted conflict or as a tourist paradise, neither of which attends to the native expressions of attachment to the land as a place. Geography matters, not for the simplistic and overused reason that everything happens in space, but because where things happen is critical to knowing how and why they happen. As Robert Tally has identified that globalisation, enhanced mobility, geographic anxiety, and displacement have augmented spatial confusion, making mapping and other spatial practices increasingly significant. The Kashmiri Pandits&rsquo identity as Kashmiris has diminished in modern times, facing existential threats due to post-1989 communal tensions and mass dislocation. In this context, it is essential to focus on the spatial turn, which anchors the abstract global currents of displacement and conflict within the physical &lsquostratigraphies&rsquo (the successive layers of history and memory embedded in place), thereby transforming spaces as archives to restore human agency and identity. Geocriticism, as a field of study in Spatial Humanities, moves beyond merely plotting coordinates, allowing critics to uncover hidden social and political relations within a text&rsquos spatial dynamics rather than relying solely on referential geography. Drawing on the geocritical framework, the proposed study offers a stratigraphic and intertextual lens that foregrounds the subjectivities of Kashmiri Pandits, underscoring their particular positions within the socio-cultural space of Kashmir. It helps to examine the movements in real space, whose traces are recorded in literary and media spaces. Through readings of selected memoirs, documentaries, and photographic archives, the analysis offers insights into the themes of home, postmemory, embodied experience, and landscape of absence. In short, the study moves beyond exclusive victimhood narrative to highlight a more relational understanding of violence, displacement, and possibilities for restorative healing.

Keywords: Kashmir Kashmiri Pandits geocriticism spatial movement postmemory home
